artists.biography:
Charles "Charlie" Parker, Jr. (August 29, 1920 – March 12, 1955), also known as "Yardbird" and "Bird", was an American jazz saxophonist and composer. Miles Davis once said, "You can tell the history of jazz in four words: Louis Armstrong. Charlie Parker."
Parker acquired the nickname "Yardbird" early in his career and the shortened form, "Bird", which continued to be used for the rest of his life, inspired the titles of a number of Parker compositions, such as "Yardbird Suite", "Ornithology", "Bird Gets the Worm", and "Bird of Paradise."
Parker was a highly influential jazz soloist and a leading figure in the development of bebop, a form of jazz characterized by fast tempos, virtuosic technique, and improvisation. Parker introduced revolutionary harmonic ideas, including rapid passing chords, new variants of altered chords, and chord substitutions. His tone ranged from clean and penetrating to sweet and somber. Many Parker recordings demonstrate his virtuoso playing style and complex melodic lines, sometimes combining jazz with other musical genres, including blues, Latin, and classical.
As a teenager, Parker developed a morphine addiction while in the hospital, after an automobile accident, and subsequently became addicted to heroin. He continued using heroin throughout his life, which ultimately contributed to his death at the age of 34.
Parker was an icon for the hipster subculture and later the Beat Generation, personifying the jazz musician as an uncompromising artist and intellectual, rather than an entertainer.

perplexity.description:
Charlie Parker With Strings (Alternate Takes)" features recordings from Charlie Parker’s groundbreaking sessions with a string orchestra, originally released in 1950 on Mercury Records. These alternate takes showcase Parker’s improvisational brilliance set against lush, orchestrated arrangements, blending bebop with a more mainstream, pop-oriented sound. The album highlights Parker’s ability to navigate complex harmonic structures while maintaining his signature fluidity and emotional depth, even within the constraints of a string-laden setting. The arrangements, often criticized by jazz purists for their commercial sheen, nevertheless reveal Parker’s willingness to experiment and expand the boundaries of jazz.

This album occupies a unique place in Parker’s discography, standing apart from his small-group bebop recordings and reflecting his ambition to reach broader audiences. While some critics dismissed the string sessions as a departure from authentic jazz, others recognized them as a bold artistic move that demonstrated Parker’s versatility. The original 1950 release was commercially successful, becoming one of Parker’s best-selling albums during his lifetime. "Charlie Parker With Strings (Alternate Takes)" offers listeners a deeper look into the creative process behind these landmark recordings, capturing the nuances and spontaneity that defined Parker’s genius.
